GEOLOGY
New Paleomagnetic Data on Baltica Based on Upper Ediacaran
Deposits on the Western Slope of the Middle Urals
N. M. Fedorova, N. M. Levashova, J. G. Meert,
Corresponding Member of the RAS A. V. Maslov, and M. T. Krupenin
Received November 26, 2013
Abstract—The latest concepts about the Earth’s paleogeography for the period of 700–500 million years are
quite contradictory. Reliable paleomagnetic data are quite scarce for the Ediacaran–Cambrian of the major-
ity of continental plates, which means that making any reliable global paleogeographic and paleotectonic
reconstructions is impossible. According to various authors, Baltica within this time, for example, could have
been located at any latitudes from the South Pole to the equator. Making correct reconstructions requires new
paleomagnetic data; however, almost all objects that are applicable for such studies within Baltica have
already been studied. A possible solution is to study the deformed margins of the plate, in particular, the west-
ern megazone of the Middle Urals, where the lower and upper Ediacaran volcanogenic–sedimentary and
sedimentary sections are known within the Kvarkushsko–Kamennogorskii anticlinorium [1, 2] (Fig. 1). This
paper presents the first paleomagnetic results obtained for the sedimentary rocks of the Upper Ediacaran
Chernokamenskaya suite. They are consistent with the group of six poles of the same age [3; 4–7], by which
Baltica was located at the subequatorial latitudes at the end of the Educarian.

Fig. 2. (A—C) are the Zijderveld diagrams for the samples from the Chernokamenskaya suite in the stratigraphic coordinate sys-
tem in the direct (A, B) and reverse (C) polarity. The shaded (unshaded) circles are the projection on the horizontal (vertical)
plane. (D and E) are the stereograms of HTC magnetization directions for the rocks from the Chernokamenskaya suite in the
geographic (D) and stratigraphic (E) coordinates. The shaded (unshaded) circles are the directions of the direct (reverse) polarity.
(1) high-temperature component (HTC), (2) average temperature component (ATC); (3) mean direction of the HTC with a con-

text); (2) poles aged approximately 555 million years, the southeastern coast of the White Sea [12–14]; (3) is the pole aged 540–550
million years for the volcanic rocks from the Southern Volyn’ [15]; (4) is the pole aged 540–550 million years for the sedimentary rocks
from the Southern Urals [11]; (5) is the pole for the secondary component in the rocks from the Chernokamenskaya suite.
